title: Research
text:
Youth Gang Involvement and Criminal Offending among Serious Adolescent Offenders: A Rational Choice Mediation Perspective
with S. Hong and S. Han
This study examines whether gang involvement shapes adolescents’ perceptions of the rewards and costs of offending and whether these perceptions mediate the relationship between gang involvement and subsequent criminal offending.
Data-generating process. The study uses longitudinal data from the Pathways to Desistance project, which followed 1,354 serious adolescent offenders recruited from court systems in Maricopa County, Arizona, and Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania, from adolescence into young adulthood. Participants were interviewed 11 times over approximately seven years, producing repeated measures of gang involvement, perceptions of crime-related rewards and costs, and self-reported offending.

title: Assignment 2
text:
Website Results
The five-year file covered September 2021 to September 2026, and the data were monthly. When I changed the time window to one year, the data changed to weekly.
Google Trends does not show actual search counts. The values are scaled from 0 to 100. A value of 100 represents the peak level of relative search interest within the query, while 0 represents very low relative interest.
I also removed “Election” from the original query and downloaded the data again. The values for Trump and Kamala Harris changed. This showed that the values are rescaled depending on which search terms are included in the query.

title: Assignment 2
text:
Google Trends in R
I also collected Google Trends data using the gtrendsR package in R. The R object contained more information than the website CSV. It included interest by country, region, DMA, and city, as well as related topics and related queries.

library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)

TrumpHarrisElection <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

the_df <- TrumpHarrisElection$interest_over_time

write_csv(
  the_df,
  paste0("gtrends_us_5y_", Sys.Date(), ".csv")
)


library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

cached_data <- read_csv(
  "gtrends_us_5y_2026-09-09.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

cached_data$hits_num <- parse_number(cached_data$hits)

ggplot(cached_data,
       aes(x = date, y = hits_num, color = keyword)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Google Trends Interest Over Time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Search interest",
    color = "Search term"
  )








I compared “Kamala Harris” and “Harris,” and the two series were not the same. “Harris” is a broader search term and can include searches that are not about Kamala Harris. This showed that the search term used can affect what is actually being measured.

title: Assignment 2
text:
Comparing the Two Methods
The website and R results were not exactly the same. For example, for September 2021, the website value for Trump was 4, while the R-based value was 1, which was 3 points lower.
The R method was easier to reproduce because the search settings were written directly in the code. It would also be easier to use R if I needed to collect data for many search terms. With the website method, I had to record the search settings manually.
Both methods can also have problems. The website interface can change, while gtrendsR depends on an unofficial service and may be affected by rate limits or changes to Google Trends.
I ran the same gtrendsR call twice a few minutes apart. In my run, the two results were identical. However, Google Trends uses sampled search data, so repeated pulls are not guaranteed to always return the same values.

title: Assignment 1
text:
Website Design
This website was created using RStudio and Quarto and is published through GitHub Pages. I used the Cosmo theme because it provides a clean and professional appearance that is appropriate for an academic website.
The navigation bar is organized so that visitors can easily access the main sections of the website. The Home page provides a brief introduction and summarizes my research interests. The Research page presents my current research and working papers, while the Teaching page summarizes my teaching experience. The CV page provides access to my current curriculum vitae, and the Assignments menu contains course-related materials.
I chose a simple layout with minimal visual elements so that the focus remains on the content. I also considered readability and ease of navigation when designing the website. The colors, fonts, and overall structure are kept simple and consistent across the pages. Because the primary purpose of the website is to present my academic work, I wanted visitors to be able to quickly find information about my research, teaching, and CV without unnecessary visual elements.
The website also includes direct links to my GitHub profile and email address so that visitors can easily find additional information or contact me. The same navigation structure is used across the website to provide a consistent user experience.
The website was built as a Quarto project in RStudio. The rendered HTML files are stored in the docs folder and published through GitHub Pages. This structure allows me to update the website by editing the Quarto files, rendering the site again, and pushing the updated files to GitHub.

title: Assignment 1
text: Anscombe’s four datasets may have similar statistical results, but the actual data patterns identified by graphs are very different. The first dataset shows a relatively normal linear relationship, but the second dataset shows a curved pattern. So, a simple linear regression line does not fully explain the data pattern. In the third dataset, most of the points show a consistent pattern, but one outlier strongly influences the result. Lastly, in the fourth dataset, most points are concentrated in one location, but one point strongly impacts the result. Anscombe’s four datasets show that it is difficult to fully understand the actual data pattern by just checking the mean, correlation, and regression results. Therefore, when we analyze data, it is suggested to draw graphs first and check the patterns and outliers instead of just checking the statistical results.

title: Assignment 1
text:
3. Crime Rate Chart Critique

This graph shows the trend in Index crime in the United States from 2014 to 2024, and it is good to see the changes in the overall crime rate by separating violent crime and property crime. Also, it has a good point that the graph clearly indicates that the 2021 data are not comparable with other years. However, there is also a critical point: the 2024 data are not final annual data but preliminary data estimated based on the percent change between 2023 and early 2024, but they are described in almost the same way as other years’ final data. In other words, readers can misunderstand that the 2024 data are also final data like other years. Also, the title indicates that the crime rate in 2024 is the lowest since 1961, but the graph only shows crime rates from 2014 to 2024, so the readers cannot check the long-term comparison themselves through the graph. Lastly, the total height of the bar already shows the total Index crime, but showing the same value again with a line may be redundant. Therefore, the 2024 estimated numbers should be clearly distinguished using a different color or separate annotation. Also, to support the title of long-term comparison, data from a longer time period should be presented to increase the accuracy and clarity of the graph.
Source: Prison Policy Initiative, “U.S. crime rates continue to fall, and preliminary data indicate that the 2024 crime rate was the lowest since 1961”
